title: Testing a fire detection and alarm system in an occupied building
verdict:
I would not sign it. The correction is good work and the ten findings against the last version are genuinely answered, not gestured at — steps[6] now carries the non-conductive pole, the "look at head height / that is work NEAR energised equipment, stop" rule and a real sprinkler-head control; EWP crush and overturn are named as hazards and controlled at four levels with a matching emergency paragraph and site prompt; the mobile scaffold has a control block and training[9] carries the SB licence; the fall-arrest s 80 wording no longer claims the law requires a written plan; steps[8].controls[4] is administrative where it belongs; the QFD form number and the named monitoring centre are gone. I pulled SL 2008 No. 160 and confirmed the part fix: Part 3 is "Occupancy limits for buildings" (ss 14-16) and Part 4 is "Evacuation planning, instruction and practice" (ss 17-30+), with s 19 "Meaning of person with special needs" inside it — steps[0].controls[2] is now right. I checked the one standard the correction added on its own: AS 2550.10:2025 Cranes, hoists and winches — Safe use, Part 10: Mobile elevating work platforms is real, current and correctly titled. Structurally the file is clean — twelve keys, hierarchy order holds in all twelve steps, no residual above its initial, no admin/PPE-only step claiming low, no repealed instrument standing alone. I could not render WHS Regulation s 48 or s 81 directly off legislation.qld.gov.au in this session (the section view returned only the site chrome), so those two rest on the earlier verification and on WorkSafe Qld for the SB class; flagging that rather than pretending I re-read them.

What stops the signature is not the law and not the falls work. It is that this document turns off a building's entire fire-mode response and never tells anybody. By the time step 7 is running, the zones are isolated, every ancillary output is isolated one by one, and the gaseous release is locked off at the cylinder. In that state the fire doors are held open, the shutters do not drop, the stair pressurisation and smoke exhaust do not start, the lifts do not recall and the fail-safe exit doors do not release. The occupier's written authority covers the detection system and everything that signals through the ASE — not one word about the ancillaries. The fire watch is briefed on what is "unmonitored" — the ancillaries are not unmonitored, they are dead. And the real-fire emergency paragraph restores exactly one thing, the brigade signal, and hands the chief warden an evacuation through a building whose fire-mode response the crew switched off that morning. The same document calls propping a fire door "indefensible ... while the detection system is isolated" and then holds every fire door in the building open on an isolated output for six hours without comment.

Under that sit six more real gaps. Nobody has named a hazard at the gaseous cylinder bank, though step 4 sends a technician there to pull an actuator off a charged cylinder. "Mag locks releasing on a secure area" is named in steps[4].hazards[5] and never controlled, in a document that works in aged care and child care. The occupant warning is never addressed for detector testing at all — step 5 says "put the panel in test" and never says what test mode inhibits, and step 7 gives a technician standing a metre under a sounder no hearing protection and no startle control. s 291(p) artificial extremes of temperature is declared a trigger for this job, ticked at sign-on and asked about on the prompts, and there is not one control anywhere for a cold store, a freezer room or a chiller. The EWP work never separates a boom from a scissor, so ejection is unnamed and the harness rule reads as a bar on clipping on in the one machine where clipping on is compulsory. And the roof gets a fall of more than 2m controlled by a prohibition and an undefined "restraint" with nowhere to clip, in a document that everywhere else applies s 79(3) properly. Close those and I would sign it and send a crew out on it.

blocking.field: emergency — the paragraph 'REAL FIRE WHILE THE SYSTEM IS ISOLATED'; read against steps[2].controls[1], steps[3].controls[1] and steps[4].controls[0]
blocking.problem: The procedure restores one thing: the brigade signal. Everything else the crew has switched off stays off. By step 7 this building typically has zone isolates applied (steps[2].controls[1] 'Isolate zone by zone ... so the unmonitored footprint is as small as the job allows'), every ancillary output isolated individually (steps[4].controls[0]), and the gaseous, pre-action and deluge release locked off at the cylinder (steps[3].controls[1]). In a real fire at that moment the fire doors on hold-open devices stay open, the fire and smoke shutters do not drop, the smoke exhaust and stair pressurisation do not start, the lifts do not recall, the fail-safe exit doors do not release and the zone under test does not detect. The paragraph says to take the ASE off isolate, 'run the panel's evacuate function' and 'name any space whose suppression is locked off'. It never says to clear the zone isolates, it never says to de-isolate the ancillaries, and it never tells the chief warden which fire-mode functions will not work while he walks people down a stair that is not pressurised, through fire doors that are still held open. The same document calls propping a fire door 'indefensible ... while the detection system is isolated' (steps[9].controls[2]) and then holds every fire door in the building open on an isolated output all day without a word. A crew reading this believes 'ASE back on' is the emergency action. It is the least of them.
blocking.fix: Rewrite the paragraph so the restoration is ordered and the warden is told, in this order: (1) 'Clear the zone isolates and take the ASE off isolate — the panel has to be able to see the fire and send it.' (2) 'De-isolate the ancillaries next. They are what protects the people walking out: door holders release so the fire doors shut, shutters drop, smoke exhaust and stair pressurisation start, lifts recall, exit doors release. Take the group off if the panel will do it, one at a time if it will not, and say out loud what you have restored.' (3) 'Tell the chief warden in plain words what is still not working and what is still locked off — name the doors, the stairs and any protected space whose suppression is off — before he starts moving people. He is running the evacuation on what you tell him.' (4) 'The gaseous and pre-action release stays locked off unless the FM tells you to restore it and the protected space is clear of people — say to 000 and to the first officer in which space has no suppression.' Then keep the existing 'stand at the FIP with the keys, the block plan and the zone in alarm'.

blocking.field: steps[3] ('4. Lock off gaseous, pre-action and deluge release before any detector in a protected space is touched') — hazards[] carries nothing about the cylinder bank, against controls[1] and controls[2]
blocking.problem: All seven hazards in this step are about the protected space — discharge into it, oxygen depletion in it, pressure surge in it, discharge noise in it. The step's own instructions then send the technician somewhere else entirely and put his hands on a charged system: controls[1] 'solenoid or actuator disconnected from the cylinder ... VERIFY IT WITH YOUR OWN EYES AT THE CYLINDER BANK', controls[2] 'Confirm no pyrotechnic or squib actuator remains connected'. Disconnecting an actuator off a charged cylinder is the most dangerous minute in this job and the room he is standing in is not a named hazard: discharge at the bank while he is on it, a mechanical manual release lever knocked on the master cylinder, an inert gas or CO2 flood in a small cylinder room with the door shut behind him, an unrestrained or uncapped cylinder. training[6] requires competence on the system type, which helps, and controls[2] hands a pyrotechnic actuator to the gaseous contractor — but the crew is given no method for the bank itself.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[3].hazards: 'Discharge at the cylinder bank while the actuator is being disconnected' and 'Asphyxiation in a cylinder room — an inert gas or CO2 bank discharging into the room you are standing in'. Add to steps[3].controls in hierarchy order: (isolate) 'Secure the mechanical manual release on the master cylinder first — pin or lock it and see it done — before your hands go near the actuator. That lever fires the system on its own and does not care what the panel says.' (isolate) 'Cylinders stay restrained in their brackets with the safety cap or anti-recoil fitting on where one is supplied. Nothing gets disconnected from a discharge hose to prove anything.' (administrative) 'Nobody disconnects an actuator alone. A second person stays at the cylinder room door, keeps it from latching without wedging it, and can get you out. Never stand in front of a discharge outlet, an open port or a disconnected actuator.' (administrative) 'On a CO2 bank you do not do the isolation — the gaseous contractor does, and you watch from outside the room. A CO2 discharge in a cylinder room kills before you reach the door.'

blocking.field: steps[4] ('5. Isolate ancillary outputs one at a time and put the panel in test') — controls[] as a whole; read against permits[0], steps[0].controls[3] and steps[2].controls[6]-[8]
blocking.problem: Step 3 has a discipline for the brigade isolate that step 5 does not have for the ancillaries: a written authority naming what is off, a tag on the panel door, a time on, a maximum time off, two phone alarms, and a fire watch briefed in person. The occupier's written authority (permits[0], steps[0].controls[3]) covers 'the fire detection and alarm system, the ASE and every other system that signals through that ASE' — the ancillary outputs are not in it. The fire watch is briefed on 'everything now unmonitored' (steps[2].controls[8]) — the ancillaries are not unmonitored, they are disabled, and a fire watch told to watch for smoke has no idea the fire doors are open and the stairs are not pressurised. There is no tag, no maximum period and no clock on the ancillary isolation. So the occupier authorises one thing, the crew does a larger thing, and the only two people in the building who know the fire-mode response is off are the two technicians.
blocking.fix: Extend the existing discipline rather than inventing a new one. In steps[4].controls, add (administrative) 'The ancillary outputs you isolate go on the same written authority as the ASE, listed individually — lifts, AHU, smoke exhaust, stair pressurisation, shutters, door holders, mag locks — with a maximum period, the same as the brigade signal. If it is not on the authority you do not isolate it.' Add (administrative) 'Brief the fire watch and the chief warden on the ancillaries before the first one goes off, in plain words: which fire doors will stay open, which shutters will not drop, that the stairs will not pressurise, that the lifts will not recall, and that the exit doors will not release. They are running the building on what you told them.' Add (administrative) 'Same tag, same clock: what is isolated, time on, expected off, maximum off, your name. If the job overruns the maximum, the ancillaries go back on before anything else.' Amend permits[0] and steps[0].controls[3] to name the ancillary outputs alongside the ASE, and add a siteSpecificPrompt: 'Which ancillary outputs will be isolated today, for how long, who has been told, and what does the building lose while they are off?'

blocking.field: steps[4] ('... and put the panel in test') and steps[6] ('7. Test detectors, manual call points and beam, duct or aspirating devices') — no control in either step addresses the occupant warning, and steps[6].controls[21] is the PPE line
blocking.problem: The document spends two whole steps making sure the building is never startled by an alarm it was not told about, then tests every detector in the building without once saying what the occupant warning does when a device operates. Step 5's title says 'put the panel in test' and not one of its eight controls says what test mode is, whether it inhibits the alarm and ancillary outputs, or that it must be proved on the display first — the exact discipline the document applies rigorously to the brigade isolate ('Read the display back' at steps[2].controls[0]; 'confirm on the panel type in front of you exactly what the isolate inhibits ... and prove it on the display' at steps[2].controls[4]). If the panel is not in a walk-test mode that silences and auto-resets, every detector test in step 7 runs the full occupant warning — which is the outcome steps[1] and steps[2] exist to prevent. And a sounder is routinely within a metre of the detector being tested: steps[6].controls[21] lists 'Glasses, gloves, P2 mask ... hard hat' and no hearing protection, and nothing in the step covers a full-volume alarm going off beside a technician's head while he is on a platform ladder or in an EWP basket at ceiling height. All the noise and startle controls sit in step 8, a different step run at a different time.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[4].controls, with the other isolate controls: 'Put the panel in its one-man test / walk-test mode and prove on the display what it inhibits on this panel type — occupant warning, ancillaries, brigade path — before you leave the panel. If the panel has no mode that silences the occupant warning on actuation, the alarm outputs are isolated separately and proved, or the chief warden and reception are briefed that every device test will sound the building.' Add to steps[6].hazards: 'The occupant warning sounding at full volume beside your head while you are on a ladder or in a basket at ceiling height'. Add to steps[6].controls (administrative) 'Know what the device you are about to operate will do before you operate it. If the sounder next to it will run, hearing protection is on and both feet are settled before you key it — you do not want to be reaching off a ladder when it goes.' Add hearing protectors to steps[6].controls[21].

blocking.field: hrcw[5] (WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 291(p)) and whenRequired ('s 291(p) artificial extremes of temperature — YES for detectors in cold stores, freezer rooms and chillers'), siteSpecificPrompts[18] — no matching control in any of the twelve steps
blocking.problem: The document declares artificial extremes of temperature a high risk construction work trigger for this job, tells the crew to 'tick the ones that apply on the site prompts and brief them at sign-on', asks about it on the prompts — and then gives them nothing to brief. Search all twelve steps: there is not one word about a cold store, a freezer room or a chiller. Step 10 covers heat only, and says so explicitly ('roof spaces and risers done early in the day', 'Nobody works a roof space alone in the afternoon in summer'). Nothing on how long you stay in a blast freezer, nothing on clothing, nothing on the door latch and the internal release, nothing on the ammonia or CO2 refrigerant in a cold store plant room, nothing on ice underfoot on a ladder. A technician ticks s 291(p) at sign-on, is told he is doing high risk construction work, and is handed no method for it. Step 10's 'prove it opens from the inside' rule is aimed at plant room and riser doors and no crew will read a freezer door into it.
blocking.fix: Add a control block to steps[9] (it already owns spaces you can be shut into), or a short step of its own. In hierarchy order: (eliminate) 'Test a cold store or freezer head from outside the space where the device type and the panel let you — a cold-room detector you can actuate from the warm side does not need you in the room.' (isolate) 'Before the door shuts behind you, find the internal release and operate it. No internal release, no entry — the door is held open by a person, never a wedge.' (administrative) 'Freezer and cold store work is timed and buddied: agreed time in, someone at the door who can see you, out at the agreed time whether you are finished or not. Nobody is in a freezer alone.' (administrative) 'Cold store plant rooms carry ammonia or CO2 refrigerant. If there is a refrigerant alarm, a smell of ammonia or ice on a line, back out and get the refrigeration contractor — that is not your system and not this SWMS.' (ppe) 'Insulated gloves, a jacket and a hat that leave you able to work — you lose dexterity fast at minus twenty, and a slip off a ladder on an icy floor is the injury.' Add a matching siteSpecificPrompt on the internal release, the buddy and the time.

blocking.field: steps[6].controls[19] and controls[20], and steps[6].hazards[] — read against training[10] ('EWPA Yellow Card for a boom under 11 m')
blocking.problem: The correction has made an EWP the preferred fall prevention device and controls it well for crush, overturn, ground person and set-up. It never distinguishes a boom from a scissor lift, and the two machines have different rules. In a boom-type platform the operator wears a harness with an adjustable lanyard to the manufacturer's anchor from the moment he steps in — the mechanism is being catapulted out when the boom is struck or a wheel drops into a penetration, and it is the reason the anchor is there. training[10] contemplates 'a boom under 11 m', so booms are in scope. steps[6].hazards names crush (hazards[9]) and overturn (hazards[10]) and never names ejection. Worse, controls[19] reads as a prohibition on clipping on at all: 'Fall arrest is the LAST RESORT under WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 79(3)(c) ... Nobody clips on until ALL of the following exist: a written rescue plan for this location ... No rescue plan, no harness, no work at that device.' A technician in a boom basket following this SWMS either does not wear the harness the machine requires, or wears it in breach of a rule the document states in capitals. That is one control prohibiting what another requires.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[6].hazards: 'Ejected from a boom-type EWP basket when the boom is struck or a wheel drops'. Split the harness rule by machine type. Add, with the engineering controls: 'Boom-type EWP: harness and adjustable lanyard to the manufacturer's anchor in the basket, on before the basket leaves the floor and on until it is back down. That is not the last resort — it is part of the machine, and it is what stops you being thrown out when the boom is struck. Scissor lift: guardrails are the fall protection; no harness unless the manufacturer calls for one.' Then reword controls[19] to say plainly that the s 79(3)(c) last-resort rule and the s 80 rescue-plan gate apply to fall arrest AT A DEVICE — a harness clipped to building steel off a ladder or a walkway — not to the restraint lanyard in a boom basket, where the means of rescue is the ground controls the ground person has already operated under controls[12]. Same split in controls[20] and ppe[9]. The safe-use rule for boom-type platforms is in AS 2550.10:2025, already carried at references[26] — cite the standard by designation and do not invent a clause number for it.

blocking.field: steps[9].hazards[4] ('Fragile roof sheeting and unguarded roof edges') and steps[9].controls[6]
blocking.problem: This is a fall of more than 2m — the same hazard step 7 spends eleven controls, a passage of whenRequired and a s 299(4) record on. On the roof it gets one sentence: 'Roof access only through the permanent access and along the walkway. No stepping on unsupported sheeting, nothing on a roof in a storm or on wet sheeting, no work near an unguarded edge without restraint and the step 7 rescue-plan gate satisfied.' A prohibition and a harness. No higher control is considered at all — no temporary edge protection or guardrail, no covers or crawl boards over fragile sheeting and skylights, no static line, no 'stay 2m back from the edge and you need nothing' rule. And nothing says where you clip: step 7 is careful to say 'a rated anchor or the EWP basket anchor, never the handrail' (controls[20]), step 10 says only 'restraint'. A technician on a Queensland warehouse roof at a smoke exhaust fan, told he must be in restraint and given no anchor, improvises one. That is how people go off an edge attached to nothing. Step 7 also makes the crew record device by device why the higher controls were not reasonably practicable (controls[15], citing s 299(4)); step 10 asks for no such record for the roof, though the same subsection applies to the same kind of fall.
blocking.fix: Rewrite steps[9].controls[6] as a short hierarchy that matches step 7. (eliminate/substitute) 'Can the device be reached from inside, off the walkway, or from a platform that already has edge protection? Do that.' (engineering) 'Fragile sheeting and skylights: covers or crawl boards over them, or the area fenced off — you do not walk on them and you do not trust a purlin line you cannot see.' (engineering) 'Where work has to happen near an unguarded edge, temporary edge protection goes up first if the roof will take it.' (ppe) 'Restraint only where edge protection is not reasonably practicable: a lanyard set short so you physically cannot reach the edge, clipped to a rated and identifiable anchor or a proprietary static line — never a vent, a pipe, a duct or a sheeting screw. No rated anchor, no restraint, no work at that device: mark it untested with the reason and escalate.' Then add: 'Record device by device why the higher controls were not reasonably practicable on this roof — the same record s 299(4) requires and step 7 already makes you keep.' Add a siteSpecificPrompt: 'On this roof — walkway, fragile sheeting or skylights, rated anchors, and where exactly are they?'

blocking.field: steps[4].hazards[5] ('Mag locks releasing on a secure area or failing secure on an exit') — no matching control in steps[4].controls[]
blocking.problem: Named and then abandoned. controls[0] is a generic 'Isolate each ancillary output individually against the site's cause-and-effect matrix'; controls[1] to controls[7] cover lifts, shutters, fans, door holders and AHUs by name and never come back to mag locks. Both halves of the hazard matter. Release on a secure area: this SWMS works in aged care, ICU and child care by its own account (steps[0].hazards[2], steps[7].controls[7]), and in a memory support unit, a mental health ward or a custodial area the mag locks are the thing keeping a person inside. Dropping them on a cause-and-effect test with nobody at the door is a resident on the street, and the document's own s 19 'person with special needs' control at steps[7].controls[7] covers the sounders but not the doors. Fail secure on an exit: an exit door that does not release leaves people behind a locked door in a fire. steps[8].controls[6] proves release and re-secure at step 9, which catches the second failure after the fact and does nothing about the first.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[4].controls, with the other isolate controls: 'Access-controlled doors on a secure or restricted area — memory support unit, mental health ward, custodial area, drug room, cash room — are identified from the matrix before anything is keyed, and the FM staffs each one with a named person for the whole time the output is proved, or that door is tested out of hours with the area empty. You do not drop a mag lock on a dementia unit and go looking at the panel.' Add (administrative) 'Every mag lock on the matrix is written down before you start and ticked back at step 11 — proved to release, proved to re-secure, and pushed on by hand on the walk-off. A lock that fails secure on an exit is a critical defect, not a note for next time.' Add a matching siteSpecificPrompt: 'Which access-controlled doors are on the matrix, which of them hold a secure or restricted area, and who is standing at each one while it is proved?'

blocking.field: steps[7].controls[2] ('Audibility verification is done by the second technician standing outside the high-level field, or by meter on a stand')
blocking.problem: Labelled isolate. A separation distance a technician judges by ear is administrative, and this document says so itself twenty controls earlier: steps[6].controls[2] defines isolation as 'a physical barricade a person cannot walk through', and steps[6].controls[8] puts cones and a spotter down at administrative because 'Cones are not isolation and a spotter is not a barrier'. The same reasoning puts 'standing outside the high-level field' at administrative. Sitting it at isolate ranks it above the exposure-standard control at controls[3] and reads, to anyone auditing the hierarchy, as though the crew has an engineering-grade control on the noise when what they have is a person deciding he is far enough away. The 'meter on a stand' half genuinely removes the person and is defensible higher.
blocking.fix: Split the control. Keep at engineering: 'Audibility read off a sound level meter on a stand, so nobody has to stand in the field to take the reading.' Move to the top of the administrative block, immediately before the current controls[3]: 'Where a person has to take the reading, it is the second technician standing outside the high-level field, and nobody stands under a sounder holding a meter for longer than the reading takes. Standing back is a judgement, not a barrier — measure it once and mark where the line is.' Order within the step then stays valid.

blocking.field: steps[9] — the step title '10. Working alone in plant rooms, risers, ceiling voids and on the roof' against steps[9].controls[1] and controls[3]
blocking.problem: controls[1] says 'Two technicians for any plant room, riser, roof or ceiling-void work ... It is a standing rule, not a resourcing call to make on the day at the van, and it holds absolutely for after-hours work.' The step is titled 'Working alone in' those exact four places, and controls[3] then builds a 30-minute check-in regime with an escalation path for the worker who is in one of them on his own. A supervisor reads the title and the check-in and concludes solo entry is a method this SWMS supports and manages. A technician reads controls[1] and concludes it is banned outright. One of them is wrong on the day and the document does not say which. The check-in is a good control — it just has to be pointed at the right thing, which is the time the two of them are separated, not a licence to enter the space alone.
blocking.fix: Retitle the step to what its controls actually require, e.g. '10. Plant rooms, risers, ceiling voids and the roof — nobody in there on their own'. Reword controls[3] so the s 48 system of work covers the separation, not solo entry: 'You will be out of sight of each other — one at the panel, one in the riser. WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 48 requires a system of work that includes effective communication with the worker; it prescribes no interval. Safe QLD's system is a check-in every 30 minutes between the two of you, with a written escalation if one is missed: FM rings the plant room, then attends, then rings 000. The check-in covers the separation. It does not authorise anyone to be in a plant room, riser, ceiling void or on a roof on their own — controls[1] means what it says.'

blocking.field: emergency — no response for a bite or a sting, against steps[9].hazards[6] ('Snakes, wasps and vermin in risers and roof spaces')
blocking.problem: The hazard is named in the step. The controls against it are a torch aimed at electrical hazards (steps[9].controls[5] 'Torch into the space before your head and your hands go in') and PPE (controls[10] 'long sleeves, gloves, enclosed boots'). The emergency section runs to nine scenarios — fire, gas discharge, sprinkler head, brigade turnout, self-evacuation, failed restoration, electric shock, EWP entrapment, fall, heat illness — and covers none of it. In a Queensland roof space in September a snake bite or a wasp nest and an anaphylactic technician is a 000 call with a specific first response, and the person he is working with needs to know it before he goes up the ladder, not while he is looking it up on a phone with no signal in a riser.
blocking.fix: Add a short paragraph to emergency, in the same voice as the rest: 'BITTEN OR STUNG IN A ROOF SPACE OR RISER. Get them out and get them still — walking spreads it. Ring 000. For a snake bite: do not wash the site, do not cut it, do not use a tourniquet. Firm pressure bandage over the bite and up the whole limb, splint it, mark the time, and keep them lying down until the ambulance arrives. For a sting where they are swelling, wheezing or going grey: that is anaphylaxis — autoinjector if they carry one, into the outer thigh, then 000, and tell the operator it is anaphylaxis. Somebody meets the ambulance at the door and walks them in.'
